summary.text: The Atlantic bluefin tuna is a tuna of the western and eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean, recorded at up to 680 kg.
Prized for sushi and sashimi in Japan, it was severely overfished, with stocks falling 72% in the eastern and 82% in the western Atlantic over 40 years.
Enforced regional quotas have since raised numbers somewhat, and in 2021 it moved from Endangered to Least Concern, though many regional stocks remain severely depleted.

facts.label: Oldest individuals
facts.value: Very large ones may be up to 50 years old

items.prompt: Which tuna is the Atlantic bluefin's closest living relative?
items.explain: It is most closely related to the Pacific bluefin; the southern bluefin's resemblance comes from convergent evolution.

items.prompt: After years of overfishing, Atlantic bluefin numbers rose somewhat. What is credited for this?

options.label: A worldwide ban on its trade
A collapse in demand for sushi

items.explain: A UN proposal to ban international trade was voted down; enforcement of regional quotas has since led to some population increases.

items.prompt: In Spanish the bluefin is called atún rojo, and in Italian tonno rosso. Where does the 'red' come from?

options.label: The red fins along its back
The red colour of its meat
The Red Sea, where it was named

items.explain: In some languages the red colour of the bluefin's meat is part of its name.

items.prompt: What mainly drove the severe overfishing of the Atlantic bluefin?

options.label: Its use as bait for shark fishing
Demand for its oil to light lamps
Its value as sushi and sashimi in Japan

items.explain: Medium and large fish are heavily targeted for the Japanese raw-fish market, and this commercial importance led to severe overfishing.

items.prompt: In 2021, after quotas had helped numbers recover somewhat, how did the IUCN change the Atlantic bluefin's Red List status?

options.label: From Endangered to Extinct in the Wild

items.explain: In September 2021 it was moved from Endangered to Least Concern, although many regional stocks remain severely depleted.

items.prompt: Atlantic bluefin are native to the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. What has happened to them in the Black Sea?

options.label: They are farmed there in pens
They are more common than ever

items.explain: They have become regionally extinct in the Black Sea.

paragraphs.heading: A giant of the Atlantic
paragraphs.text: The Atlantic bluefin tuna, Thunnus thynnus, is a tuna of the family Scombridae. It lives on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean and in the Mediterranean Sea, but it has vanished from the Black Sea. Full-grown adults average 2 to 2.5 m long and about 225 to 250 kg, and the heaviest on record reached 680 kg. That puts it in the same size class as black and blue marlin and swordfish.

paragraphs.heading: Built for long journeys
paragraphs.text: Seen from the side, its body is sturdy and diamond-shaped, with a cone-shaped head and a fairly large mouth. The head holds a so-called pineal window that helps the fish find its way across a range thousands of miles wide. It is dark blue on top and gray underneath, with a gold shimmer over the body and bright yellow finlets toward the tail. Short pectoral fins set bluefin apart from related tunas, and its liver is unusual in being covered with striped blood vessels.

paragraphs.heading: Family ties
paragraphs.text: Carl Linnaeus first described the fish in 1758, under the name Scomber thynnus. Its closest relative is the Pacific bluefin tuna, and for many years the two were treated as one species, or as subspecies, called the northern bluefin tuna. The southern bluefin tuna looks similar but is actually closer to yellowfin and bigeye tuna. Scientists put that likeness down to convergent evolution rather than close kinship, and many of the shared features are adaptations to cold water.

paragraphs.heading: A prized catch
paragraphs.text: People have valued this fish as food throughout recorded history, and its size, speed and power as a hunter have won admirers among fishermen, writers and scientists. It supports one of the world's most profitable fisheries, and medium and large fish are heavily sought for Japan's raw-fish market, where bluefin is prized for sushi and sashimi. Commercial crews catch it with longlines, purse seines, hook-and-line gear, heavy rods and harpoons. Since the 1930s it has also been a leading big-game target for sport fishermen, especially in the United States.

paragraphs.heading: Overfishing and recovery
paragraphs.text: That demand led to severe overfishing. In October 2009 the international commission that looks after Atlantic tunas confirmed that stocks had dropped over 40 years by 72% in the eastern Atlantic and 82% in the western Atlantic. Monaco then proposed listing the fish under CITES with a ban on international trade, but a later UN proposal to shield it from that trade was voted down. Since then, enforcing regional fishing quotas has helped numbers rise somewhat, and in 2021 the species moved from Endangered to Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Many regional groups remain badly depleted, though, including western fish that spawn in the Gulf of Mexico.

paragraphs.heading: Record fish and long lives
paragraphs.text: The largest bluefin taken under International Game Fish Association rules weighed 679 kg and measured 3.84 m, caught off North Lake on Prince Edward Island. In 1934, near Liverpool, Nova Scotia, six men took turns fighting a single tuna for 62 hours, the longest such contest on record. Bluefin mature fairly quickly: in one survey of fish up to 2.55 m and 247 kg, none seemed older than 15 years. Yet the very largest may live to 50.
